fichas.title: Sound Insulation, Sound Absorption, and Protection from External Noise
fichas.summary: Guidance on reducing noise from building services, including plumbing fixtures, pipework, filling and emptying sounds, heating boilers, and ventilation ducts. Sound absorption reduces reflected sound rather than sound transmitted through building components or direct sound. External-noise protection uses building layout, insulated construction and openings, blinds, and landscaping. Illustrations show pipe clips, a boiler foundation, metal/rubber elements, duct silencers, room sound absorption, and sound reduction by open-air obstructions.
spaces: Rooms containing ventilation and air-conditioning ducts
uses: Reduce plumbing fixture and pipework noise
Isolate boilers and service connections from structure
Reduce sound transmission through ventilation ducts
Reduce reflected sound and reverberation in rooms
Protect occupied rooms from external noise

Sound absorption
Sound absorption, in contrast to sound insulation, does not
normally reduce the transmission of sound through a building
component. Neither does it influence the sound, which reaches
the ear directly from the source; it only reduces the reflected
sound. Because the direct sound reduces with distance from the
source, the reflected sound is just as loud or louder than the direct
sound outside an 'echo' radius around the sound source ---7 0.
If sound reflection is reduced, then the level of reflected sound
sinks outside the previous echo radius. The sound absorption
capacity of a room is given in m2 of equivalent sound absorption
area, the ideal sound-absorbing area, which would have the same
absorption capacity as the room itself. (For a reverberation time of
1.5 s, the equivalent sound-absorbing area (A) would have to be
0.1 m2 per m3 of room volume M; for half the reverberation time,
it would be twice the size.)
Protection from external noise
The best protection against noise from outside (traffic noise, etc.):
appropriate design of the building - occupied rooms positioned
on the side away from the noise; sound-insulated construction of
the external walls; above all, sound-insulated doors and windows;
installation of sound-insulating blinds on the fagade side; and
sound protection through landscaping (embankments, walls,
planting). The sound reduction effect of these measures can be
read from ---7 0 for various wavelengths (wavelength approx.
340 m/frequency).

normally reduce the transmission of sound through a building
component. Neither does it influence the sound, which reaches
the ear directly from the source; it only reduces the reflected
sound. Because the direct sound reduces with distance from the
source, the reflected sound is just as loud or louder than the direct
sound outside an 'echo' radius around the sound source ---7 0.
If sound reflection is reduced, then the level of reflected sound
sinks outside the previous echo radius. The sound absorption
capacity of a room is given in m2 of equivalent sound absorption
area, the ideal sound-absorbing area, which would have the same
absorption capacity as the room itself. (For a reverberation time of
1.5 s, the equivalent sound-absorbing area (A) would have to be
0.1 m2 per m3 of room volume M; for half the reverberation time,
it would be twice the size.)
Protection from external noise
The best protection against noise from outside (traffic noise, etc.):
appropriate design of the building - occupied rooms positioned
on the side away from the noise; sound-insulated construction of
the external walls; above all, sound-insulated doors and windows;
installation of sound-insulating blinds on the fagade side; and
sound protection through landscaping (embankments, walls,
planting). The sound reduction effect of these measures can be
read from ---7 0 for various wavelengths (wavelength approx.
340 m/frequency).
